# `react/prefer-lazy-state-init`

**useState's initial value is not computed on every render**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-react` (npm) · `codelaw-rules-react` (PyPI) |
| **Languages** | JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:react/recommended` at `warn` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `suggest` — `codelaw fix --unsafe` applies it; review the diff, it can change behaviour (wrapping changes behaviour when the value is itself a function, and moves the call's side effects to the first render only) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.3.0 |
| **Ported from** | `@eslint-react/use-state` |

## What it checks

`useState`'s argument doesn't call a function or construct an object on every render:
`useState(load())` and `useState(new Map())` compute a value that React uses only on the first
render. Pass a function instead — `useState(() => load())` — and React calls it once. Calls of
hooks, of `Boolean`, `String` and `Number`, of a method (`JSON.parse(…)`), and calls inside
`use(…)` or inside a function are not reported.

**Why:** The argument is evaluated on every render even though React ignores it after the first, so an expensive call runs for nothing each time.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-react
pip install codelaw-rules-react
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:react/recommended` sets it to `warn`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:react/recommended"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"react/prefer-lazy-state-init" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "react/prefer-lazy-state-init" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"react/prefer-lazy-state-init" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"react/prefer-lazy-state-init" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"react/prefer-lazy-state-init" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "react/prefer-lazy-state-init": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **JavaScript:** `// codelaw-ignore react/prefer-lazy-state-init: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore react/prefer-lazy-state-init expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule react/prefer-lazy-state-init --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain react/prefer-lazy-state-init       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule react/prefer-lazy-state-init  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>                # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## Examples

### JavaScript

#### Don't

```js
function useTodos() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState(loadTodos());
  return [todos, setTodos];
}
```

#### Do

```js
function useTodos() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState(() => loadTodos());
  return [todos, setTodos];
}
```

### JSX

#### Don't

```jsx
function Cart() {
  const [items] = useState(new Map());
  return <p>{items.size}</p>;
}
```

#### Do

```jsx
function Cart() {
  const [items] = useState(() => new Map());
  return <p>{items.size}</p>;
}
```

### TypeScript

#### Don't

```ts
function useFilters() {
  const [filters, setFilters] = useState({ tags: readTags() });
  return [filters, setFilters] as const;
}
```

#### Do

```ts
function useFilters() {
  const [filters, setFilters] = useState(() => ({ tags: readTags() }));
  return [filters, setFilters] as const;
}
```

### TSX

#### Don't

```tsx
function Editor() {
  const [doc] = useState(createDocument());
  return <article>{doc.title}</article>;
}
```

#### Do

```tsx
function Editor() {
  const [doc] = useState(() => createDocument());
  return <article>{doc.title}</article>;
}
```

## Differences from the source

- This is the lazy-initialisation part of @eslint-react's `use-state`; its other two checks — that the call is destructured, and that the setter is named `set` + the value's name — are naming conventions, not ported here.
- Upstream reports each call in the argument; codelaw reports the argument once, naming the first call, and offers one fix for it.
